title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Events Sector (UK events management, conferences, exhibitions, festivals, event production, staging/AV hire)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency in the UK events industry 2023-2026 — deposit/advance-booking exposure and deferred income, thin project margins, supplier prepayments, high fixed overheads on venues/staff, seasonality and cancellation risk, rising staging/AV/energy/insurance costs, and slow post-pandemic recovery of corporate and consumer event budgets? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK events-sector companies (event management agencies, conference/exhibition organisers, festival operators, event production/staging firms) that entered administration, CVL or other insolvency between 2023 and 2026 — give company name, month/year, procedure, and stated cause. Include festival cancellations/insolvencies and any notable exhibition or agency failures. Verify from London Gazette, insolvency practitioner notices, or trade press (Access All Areas, Conference News, Festival Insights).

How do UK events businesses appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm events activities sit largely in SIC section R (arts, entertainment and recreation, e.g. division 90 creative/arts/entertainment, 93 sports/amusement/recreation) and section N (82.30 organisation of conventions and trade shows). Note the Insolvency Service does not isolate an 'events' sub-total and figures are England and Wales only, not UK.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK events business is heading toward insolvency — negative working capital masked by client deposits held as deferred income, reliance on the next event's deposits to pay the last event's suppliers, supplier credit tightening or pro-forma demands, VAT/PAYE arrears, and margin erosion on won pitches? Frame as indicators, not proof of insolvency.

What insolvency and rescue options apply to UK events companies specifically, and what sector complexities arise — treatment of customer deposits and pre-sold ticket money in a CVL/administration (are ticket-holders and deposit-payers unsecured creditors?), consumer prepayment protection, contracts with venues and suppliers, retention of key creditor and client relationships, and when a CVA or administration sale of the agency/brand is realistic? Moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.

title: Insolvency and Business Rescue for the Taxi and Private Hire Sector (UK taxi firms, private hire operators, minicab fleets, PHV operators)
research_questions: What are the specific structural and financial drivers of insolvency for UK taxi and private hire operators 2023-2026 — competition from app-based platforms (Uber/Bolt) compressing margins, driver shortages and driver acquisition costs, vehicle finance and lease exposure on fleets, the shift to electric/ULEZ-compliant vehicles and capital cost, fuel and insurance cost rises, and local-authority licensing costs? Cite sources and dates.

Name specific UK taxi or private hire companies that entered administration, CVL or other insolvency between 2023 and 2026 — company name, month/year, procedure, and stated cause. Include any notable regional minicab/PHV operator failures and fleet operators. Verify from London Gazette, insolvency notices, or trade/local press.

How do UK taxi and private hire businesses appear in the Insolvency Service company insolvency statistics for England and Wales by SIC section? Confirm they sit in SIC section H (transport and storage), division 49 land transport, class 49.32 taxi operation. Note the Insolvency Service reports at section level for E&W and does not isolate a taxi sub-total, and section H also contains haulage/freight; figures are England and Wales only.

What are the earliest reliable warning signs that a UK taxi/private hire operator is heading toward insolvency — falling driver numbers and rising empty-vehicle costs, missed vehicle-finance or lease payments, HMRC (VAT/PAYE) arrears, VAT treatment uncertainty on operator commissions, and cashflow strain from insurance renewals? Frame as indicators, not proof.

What insolvency and rescue options apply to UK taxi/private hire companies specifically, and what sector complexities arise — treatment of vehicle finance/HP/lease agreements and asset repossession in a CVL or administration, operator licence continuity, driver (usually self-employed) status and any employment claims, and when restructuring vs closure makes sense? Moderate all legal claims for a YMYL audience.
